content: The etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol vaginal ring is a contraceptive device that combines estrogen and progestin to prevent pregnancy. It is FDA-approved for this purpose. The ring is inserted into the vagina and remains in place for three weeks, followed by a one-week break during which withdrawal bleeding typically occurs. A new ring is then inserted to continue the cycle. The exact position of the ring in the vagina is not critical for its effectiveness, and it can be inserted in a position most comfortable for the user, such as standing with one leg raised, squatting, or lying down. The ring should be compressed and inserted into the vagina, and it can be removed by hooking a finger under the rim or grasping it between two fingers. If the ring is accidentally expelled and remains outside the vagina for less than three hours, contraceptive efficacy is not reduced. It should be rinsed with cool or lukewarm water and reinserted as soon as possible. If the ring is lost, a new one should be inserted immediately, and the regimen should continue without alteration. If the ring is out of the vagina for more than three continuous hours during weeks 1 or 2, contraceptive efficacy may be reduced, and a barrier method such as condoms with spermicide should be used until the ring has been in place continuously for seven days. During week 3, if the ring is out for more than three hours, it should be discarded, and a new ring should be inserted immediately to start a new three-week cycle, or a new ring should be inserted no later than seven days after the previous ring was removed or expelled. The ring is contraindicated in women with a high risk of arterial or venous thrombosis, such as those who smoke and are over 35 years old, have a history of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, cerebrovascular or coronary artery disease, thrombogenic valvular or rhythm disorders, uncontrolled hypertension, diabetes with vascular disease, or certain types of migraines. It is also contraindicated in women with liver disease, liver tumors, breast cancer, or unexplained abnormal uterine bleeding, as well as in those who are pregnant or hypersensitive to any of the ring's components. The use of the ring should be discontinued if an arterial or venous thrombotic event occurs, if there is unexplained loss of vision or other symptoms suggestive of retinal vein thrombosis, or if jaundice develops. Women with a history of depression should be monitored carefully, and the ring should be discontinued if depression recurs to a serious degree. The ring is not recommended for women with conditions that make the vagina more susceptible to irritation or ulceration, as vaginal or cervical erosion or ulceration has been reported in some users. The ring may interfere with the correct placement of a diaphragm, so diaphragms are not recommended as a backup method. However, the use of tampons does not affect the systemic absorption of the hormones released by the ring. Women using the ring should have an annual visit with their healthcare provider for a blood pressure check and other indicated healthcare. The ring is associated with an increased risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) and arterial thrombosis, such as stroke and myocardial infarction, particularly in women with other risk factors. The risk of VTE is highest during the first year of use and after restarting the ring following a break of at least four weeks. The risk of VTE gradually disappears after discontinuation of the ring. Women with a history of pregnancy-related cholestasis or gallbladder disease may be at increased risk of these conditions while using the ring. Additionally, the ring may exacerbate symptoms of hereditary angioedema in susceptible women. Unscheduled bleeding or spotting may occur, especially during the first three months of use. If bleeding persists or occurs after previously regular cycles, other causes such as pregnancy or malignancy should be ruled out. If scheduled withdrawal bleeding does not occur, pregnancy should be considered, particularly if the prescribed dosing schedule has not been followed. Some women may experience amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea after discontinuing the ring, especially if these conditions were pre-existing. The ring is contraindicated in women with breast cancer or other estrogenor progestin-sensitive cancers. While some studies have suggested an increased risk of cervical cancer or intraepithelial neoplasia with combined hormonal contraceptives (CHCs), the extent to which these findings are due to differences in sexual behavior and other factors is controversial. The estrogen component of CHCs may raise serum concentrations of certain binding globulins, potentially necessitating adjustments in replacement thyroid hormone or cortisol therapy. Women with a history of chloasma should avoid sun or ultraviolet radiation exposure while using the ring, as chloasma may occasionally occur. The ring has been associated with cases of toxic shock syndrome (TSS), although a causal relationship has not been established. If a patient exhibits signs or symptoms of TSS, appropriate medical evaluation and treatment should be initiated. In rare cases, the ring has been inadvertently inserted into the urinary bladder, requiring cystoscopic removal. Women presenting with persistent urinary symptoms and an inability to locate the ring should be assessed for this possibility. Extensive epidemiological studies have not shown an increased risk of birth defects in women who have used oral contraceptives prior to pregnancy, nor do they suggest a teratogenic effect when taken inadvertently during early pregnancy. The ring should be discontinued if pregnancy is confirmed.
